title: the serpent-arrows and Garuda
hook: a great wind over the battlefield, and the snakes let go
carry: I'm your friend, don't ask why

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's arrows held the brothers down, Sita was flown over the field to despair, and your line, they're alive, and holding on, Trijata's signs of life. Did you offer someone one steady thing? Today, help arrives from the sky. Day six hundred forty-three.

Night on the battlefield, and the camp is out of ideas. Rama lies bound beside his brother. Sugriva wants to carry them home. Sushena, the monkey physician, says there are healing herbs on mountains far away in the ocean of milk, and someone should be sent. And while they're still talking, the wind changes. A great wind comes off the sea. Clouds tear open. The waves heave, the hills shake, and trees on the shore bend flat. Something enormous is coming down out of the sky.
screen: `OUT OF IDEAS.` → `A GREAT WIND OFF THE SEA.` → `SOMETHING COMING DOWN.`

segments.voice: It's Garuda: the great eagle, king of the birds, blazing like fire. And the moment the serpents feel him coming, they let go. The arrows that were snakes slither off the brothers and flee. In the old stories, serpents and Garuda are enemies, and the snakes don't wait to meet him. Garuda bows to the brothers. He strokes their faces with his hands, and Valmiki says their wounds close at once, their skin heals, and they rise brighter and stronger than before. Garuda embraces them both. Rama, amazed, asks: who are you? Garuda's answer is warm, and also mysterious. I'm your friend, he says, Garutman, like your own breath moving outside your body. He explains that the snakes were sons of Kadru, the mother of serpents, made into arrows by Indrajit's sorcery. And then, when you'd expect him to explain why he's come, he doesn't. Don't ask why I'm your friend, he says, more or less. You'll understand when the battle is over. He walks around Rama in a circle of respect, and flies off into the sky. The monkey army sees the brothers standing, and lets out a roar so loud that Ravana hears it inside his palace and asks what has happened. So the chapter that began with despair ends in noise. Valmiki doesn't give a speech about rescue. He gives a wind, a bird, a touch on the face, and a friend who won't say why.
screen: `GARUDA, KING OF THE BIRDS.` · `THE SERPENTS LET GO.` · `A TOUCH, AND THE WOUNDS CLOSE.` · `I'M YOUR FRIEND. DON'T ASK WHY.` · then, large: `A ROAR THAT REACHES RAVANA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath move freely. Think of a time help arrived that you didn't arrange: a neighbor at the door, a call at the right moment, a stranger who stopped. You may never have learned why they came. Remember the moment it arrived, as clearly as you can. Breathe in, and let the memory be vivid. Breathe out, and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
Garuda, the great eagle, king of birds, whose wind makes Indrajit's serpent-arrows let go of Rama and Lakshmana, and whose touch on their faces heals them completely.
Your line: I'm your friend, don't ask why. Today, when something has you wrapped tight, step outside and let the air move around you. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In recitations of the Yuddha Kanda, the Garuda episode comes straight after the brothers' fall, and tellers often slow down at Garuda's refusal to say why he came.

pairs: heard by Ravana in his palace

myth: Garuda fights the serpents in a long battle
they flee the moment they feel him coming.
Garuda heals the brothers by touching their faces
their wounds close and they rise stronger than before.
Garuda explains exactly why he came
he tells Rama not to ask, and that he'll understand after the war.

fork.setup: you're Garuda. you've freed and healed Rama, and he asks who you are and why you've come. what do you say?
options: tell him everything, from the beginning.
say you're his friend, and he'll understand later.
fork.reveal: Garuda calls himself Rama's friend, says not to ask why, and that he'll understand when the battle is over.

original.note: Sanskrit Garuḍa: the divine eagle, king of birds; Valmiki also calls him Garutmān and Suparṇa, 'fine-winged'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Garuda is simply a big bird who happened to help.
what it means: he's the king of birds, enemy of serpents, who frees and heals the brothers and calls himself Rama's friend.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki has Garuda decline to explain himself, a hint left open at this point in the war.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 50 (Sushena's advice; Garuda's arrival; the serpents flee; the brothers healed)

notes: Sarga number follows the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Sushena's proposal of herbs from mountains in the milk ocean, just before Garuda arrives: confirm.
Garuda's self-description (sakhā te garutmān … bahiścaraḥ prāṇaḥ, 'your breath moving outside'): paraphrased; confirm.
The serpents as sons of Kadru made into arrows by Indrajit's magic: confirm.
Garuda telling Rama not to ask about their friendship until after the war: paraphrased; confirm.
